note: Promotion to the tracked schema (roadmap Phase 1 backfill). Track groups follow the (XX) prefixes already embedded in the source theme names. Empty fields (track, code, level, description) are filled; authored transfer_check values replace ONLY the two known generic placeholder sentences — real source checks are never overwritten (guard in tools/normalize_blocks.py).
credential_correction: Credential correction (v0.52.0, proposed — not yet adopted by the review board): the v0.1.0 import named these tracks' credential with the bare band level 'Practitioner'. The `credential` on each track below replaces that level word only (real credential names are never overwritten); tools/normalize_blocks.py applies it as the one deliberate, counted exception to fill-empty-only and prints the count. Names follow the packs' own shape — a person and a capability, never a level word, never a job title the credential cannot confer.

bands.11–12: Conduct two real official interactions, keep the records, and coach one other person through theirs.

themes.description: Dates, names, reference numbers and copies — the personal record-keeping that wins disputes months later.
themes.transfer_check: Build a record file for one real ongoing matter — dates, names, reference numbers, copies — complete enough to hand to a stranger.

bands.K–2: Keep your important things in one folder — the letter from school, the club card — and show where it is.
bands.3–5: Start a folder for one real thing — a club, a lost item, a repair — with dates, names and copies.
bands.6–8: Build a record file for one real ongoing matter — dates, names, reference numbers, copies — and have a checker say what a stranger would still need.
bands.9–10: Build a record file for one real ongoing matter — dates, names, reference numbers, copies — complete enough to hand to a stranger.
bands.11–12: Build and use the record file to resolve a real dispute or claim, and write what the record won that memory would have lost.

themes.description: Naming what you need, choosing who to ask, and accepting help in a way that keeps your dignity and theirs.
themes.transfer_check: Make one real, specific request for help — the need named, the person chosen — and report what asking well changed.

bands.K–2: Practise saying exactly what you need help with, and say thank you.
bands.3–5: Ask one person for help with a real thing, saying exactly what you need, and tell what happened.
bands.6–8: Make one real, specific request for help — the need named, the person chosen — and tell a checker what asking well changed.
bands.9–10: Make one real, specific request for help — the need named, the person chosen — and report what asking well changed.
bands.11–12: Make a real request for help you had been avoiding, accept the help, and write what it changed for you and for them.

themes.theme: Doing something for the first time (CM)
themes.description: The method for any unfamiliar task — find someone who has done it, break it down, do the first small step today.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real unfamiliar task through the method: find someone who has done it, break it down, complete the first step today.

bands.K–2: Try one new thing with someone who knows how, and do the first small step yourself.
bands.3–5: Pick one thing you have never done, find someone who has, break it into steps, and do the first step today.
bands.6–8: Take one real unfamiliar task through the method with a checker: find someone who has done it, break it down, complete the first step today.
bands.9–10: Take one real unfamiliar task through the method: find someone who has done it, break it down, complete the first step today.
bands.11–12: Take an unfamiliar task through the method to completion, and write the method up for someone else facing a different first.

themes.theme: When you are the responsible adult (CM)
themes.description: Being the one in charge of children, elders or a situation — the duties that arrive with the role and the calls you must be ready to make.
themes.transfer_check: Run a rehearsed scenario as the responsible adult — a child, an elder, an incident — making each required call in order.

bands.K–2: Learn who to fetch and what to say when you are the biggest one in the room and something goes wrong.
bands.3–5: Practise being in charge of a younger child for a short time — the rules, the check-ins, who you call.
bands.6–8: Run a rehearsed scenario as the responsible person — a child, an elder, an incident — making each required call in order.
bands.9–10: Run a rehearsed scenario as the responsible adult — a child, an elder, an incident — making each required call in order.
bands.11–12: Run the scenario and then hold real responsibility for a person for a stated period, with the calls, the checks and the record kept.

themes.theme: Teaching somebody else what you learned (CM)
themes.description: Passing on a skill properly — showing, watching them try, and correcting without taking over.
themes.transfer_check: Teach one skill from this pack to another person, hands on their materials, until they perform it without you.

bands.K–2: Show a friend how to do one thing you can do, and let them try it themselves.
bands.3–5: Teach one skill from this pack to a classmate, hands on their things, and let them do it without you.
bands.6–8: Teach one skill from this pack to a younger learner, hands on their materials, until they perform it with only a reminder from you.
bands.9–10: Teach one skill from this pack to another person, hands on their materials, until they perform it without you.
bands.11–12: Teach one skill to two people of different ages, and write what you had to change between them.

tracks.name: The first minutes of an emergency

themes.description: The look-assess-act habit at any emergency — danger first, then the person, then the call.
themes.transfer_check: Approach three staged emergencies verbalising the sequence — danger, response, call — and act correctly in each.

bands.K–2: Learn to stop, look and fetch a grown-up when someone is hurt.
bands.3–5: Practise the three steps at a staged emergency — is it safe, is the person answering, call for help.
bands.6–8: Approach three staged emergencies saying the sequence aloud — danger, response, call — and act correctly in each with a checker watching.
bands.9–10: Approach three staged emergencies verbalising the sequence — danger, response, call — and act correctly in each.
bands.11–12: Run the three emergencies for a group of helpers, assign roles, and stop anyone about to enter an unsafe scene.

themes.description: The emergency numbers where you live, what the call-taker will ask, and giving a location that can be found.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a realistic mock emergency call: correct number, the call-taker's questions answered, your location given two ways.

bands.K–2: Learn the emergency number and practise saying your name and street.
bands.3–5: Practise the emergency call: the right number, your name, what is wrong, where you are two ways.
bands.6–8: Complete a realistic mock emergency call with a checker as call-taker: correct number, the questions answered, your location given two ways.
bands.9–10: Complete a realistic mock emergency call: correct number, the call-taker's questions answered, your location given two ways.
bands.11–12: Coach a younger person through a mock emergency call and debrief which questions they missed.

themes.description: Direct pressure, elevation and when a bleed is beyond home control — stopping blood loss with what is in reach.
themes.transfer_check: Control a staged severe bleed with correct direct pressure and escalation, narrating the decision points.

bands.K–2: Practise pressing a clean cloth on a pretend cut and holding it still until a grown-up comes.
bands.3–5: Press firmly on a staged cut with a pad, raise the arm, and keep pressing until told it has stopped.
bands.6–8: Control a staged severe bleed with correct direct pressure, narrating each decision, and say when it is beyond home control.
bands.9–10: Control a staged severe bleed with correct direct pressure and escalation, narrating the decision points.
bands.11–12: Control two staged bleeds at once, decide which needs help first, and hand over to a simulated crew with the times.

themes.description: Recognising true choking and delivering back blows and thrusts, adapted for infants and adults.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate the complete choking response on adult and infant manikins, adapting correctly for each.

bands.K–2: Learn the hands-at-the-throat sign and shout for a grown-up when you see it.
bands.3–5: Show the choking sign and practise back blows on a manikin.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate the choking response on an adult manikin and show the changes for an infant, with a checker correcting technique.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate the complete choking response on adult and infant manikins, adapting correctly for each.
bands.11–12: Manage a staged choking casualty end to end, including the change to CPR if they collapse, and teach the response to a novice.

themes.description: Cooling a burn long enough, covering it right, and the burns that must be seen by a clinician.
themes.transfer_check: Treat a staged burn with correct cooling time and covering, and state which burns must be seen by a clinician.

bands.K–2: Learn to run cool water over a small burn and to fetch a grown-up.
bands.3–5: Cool a staged burn under running water for the right time and cover it the way you were shown.
bands.6–8: Treat a staged burn with correct cooling time and covering under a checker's eye, and list the burns that must be seen by a clinician.
bands.9–10: Treat a staged burn with correct cooling time and covering, and state which burns must be seen by a clinician.
bands.11–12: Treat a staged burn on a child with the parent present, decide on the clinician, and brief them with what was done and when.

themes.description: Checking response and breathing, the recovery position, and staying until help takes over.
themes.transfer_check: Assess a staged collapse — response, breathing — place the person in the recovery position, and maintain monitoring until handover.

bands.K–2: Practise gently calling a doll's name and running for a grown-up when it does not answer.
bands.3–5: Check whether a partner answers and is breathing, and roll them onto their side the way you were shown.
bands.6–8: Assess a staged collapse — response, breathing — and place the person in the recovery position with a checker timing the monitoring.
bands.9–10: Assess a staged collapse — response, breathing — place the person in the recovery position, and maintain monitoring until handover.
bands.11–12: Assess a staged collapse, manage it through to a simulated handover, and teach the recovery position to a small group.

themes.description: Escape first, doors closed, smoke low — the household fire response, and the small fire you may fight.
themes.transfer_check: Run your dwelling's escape drill smoke-low with doors closed behind you, and state the one fire you might fight and the ones you never would.

bands.K–2: Practise crawling low to the door and getting out when the alarm sounds, and never going back in.
bands.3–5: Run the escape drill at home smoke-low with the doors closed behind you, to the meeting place.
bands.6–8: Run your dwelling's escape drill smoke-low with the doors closed behind you, timed by a checker, and state the one fire you might fight.
bands.9–10: Run your dwelling's escape drill smoke-low with doors closed behind you, and state the one fire you might fight and the ones you never would.
bands.11–12: Run the drill for a dwelling with an occupant who needs help, and write the card that names who moves whom and the fire nobody fights.

themes.description: The drowning risks around your own area, reach-and-throw rescue, and why swimmers drown trying to help.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate reach-and-throw rescue with real materials and name the three drowning risks nearest your own area.

bands.K–2: Learn to never go in the water after someone — reach with a stick or throw something that floats, and shout for a grown-up.
bands.3–5: Practise reach-and-throw rescue with a pole and a rope from the edge, never going in.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate reach-and-throw rescue with real materials under a checker, and name two drowning risks near your own area.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate reach-and-throw rescue with real materials and name the three drowning risks nearest your own area.
bands.11–12: Demonstrate reach-and-throw, assess a real local water hazard, and write the sign or card that warns the people who use it.

themes.description: Crossing, riding and travelling defensively, and the first-on-scene basics at a road accident.
themes.transfer_check: Assess one real crossing or junction for its risks and walk a staged first-on-scene response — protect, assess, call.

bands.K–2: Stop, look and listen at a real crossing with an adult, and hold hands until the road is clear.
bands.3–5: Cross a real road safely on your own using the taught method, and name two risks at your school crossing.
bands.6–8: Assess one real crossing or junction for its risks with a checker, and walk the staged first-on-scene response — protect, assess, call.
bands.9–10: Assess one real crossing or junction for its risks and walk a staged first-on-scene response — protect, assess, call.
bands.11–12: Assess a junction, walk the first-on-scene response with a group, and write the improvement request to the road authority with the evidence.

themes.description: The hours after — reporting, records, checking on people, and the reactions in yourself that are normal.
themes.transfer_check: From a staged incident, complete the after-actions: report filed, people checked, record written, and the normal reactions named.

bands.K–2: After a scary thing, tell a grown-up how you feel and know that feeling shaky is normal.
bands.3–5: After a staged incident, help check everyone is all right and say two feelings that are normal afterwards.
bands.6–8: From a staged incident, complete the after-actions with a checker — people checked, record written — and name the reactions that are normal.
bands.9–10: From a staged incident, complete the after-actions: report filed, people checked, record written, and the normal reactions named.
bands.11–12: Lead the after-actions for a group, file the report, check on people over the following days, and know when to point someone to more help.
